name: Hamlet
blurb: Shakespeare's tragedy of a Danish prince who sets out to avenge his murdered father
aka: The Tragedy of Hamlet, Prince of Denmark
title: Hamlet Summary: Plot, Characters and Ending Explained
description: Hamlet summary: who is who in Shakespeare's tragedy, what happens act by act, the ending explained, and the play's main themes and famous lines.
h1: Hamlet: Summary, Characters and Ending Explained
answer: Hamlet is a tragedy by William Shakespeare, written around 1599–1601 and first printed in 1603. It is set at the royal court of Denmark, in the castle of Elsinore. Prince Hamlet returns home after his father's sudden death to find his uncle Claudius on the throne and married to his mother, and a ghost tells him the death was murder. The play follows Hamlet as he struggles over whether, when and how to take revenge.

head: Character
Who they are
rows: Prince of Denmark, a university student called home by his father's death
Hamlet's mother, the queen, now married to Claudius
A spirit in the form of Hamlet's dead father, the old King Hamlet
The king's chief counsellor, a talkative and meddling old man
Polonius's daughter, who has been courted by Hamlet
Polonius's son, who lives in France
Two old school friends of Hamlet summoned to court by the king
Prince of Norway, leading an army near Denmark's borders

body: Act 1. King Hamlet of Denmark has died suddenly, and within two months his brother Claudius has taken the crown and married the widowed queen, Gertrude. Guards at Elsinore see a ghost that looks like the dead king, and Horatio brings Prince Hamlet to see it. The Ghost tells Hamlet that Claudius poured poison into his ear while he slept in his orchard, and demands revenge. Hamlet swears to obey and decides to act as if he were mad, so that his behaviour will not give him away.

Act 2. Polonius has ordered his daughter Ophelia to stop seeing Hamlet, and when Hamlet behaves wildly toward her, Polonius concludes that love for her has driven him mad. Claudius and Gertrude bring Rosencrantz and Guildenstern to court to find out what is wrong with the prince; Hamlet quickly sees that they are spying for the king. A company of travelling actors arrives, and Hamlet, unsure whether the Ghost is honest or a devil, plans to have them perform a play that copies his father's murder so he can watch Claudius's reaction.

Act 3. While Claudius and Polonius secretly listen, Hamlet meets Ophelia and cruelly tells her to go to a nunnery. At the play, The Murder of Gonzago, Claudius stops the performance and storms out, which Hamlet takes as proof of guilt. Soon after, Hamlet finds Claudius alone trying to pray, but holds back from killing him, reasoning that a man killed at prayer might go to heaven. In Gertrude's private room Hamlet confronts his mother; hearing a voice behind a wall hanging, he stabs through it and kills Polonius, who was hiding there. The Ghost appears again, seen only by Hamlet, to remind him of his purpose.

Act 4. Claudius sends Hamlet to England with Rosencrantz and Guildenstern, carrying a sealed letter asking the English king to execute him. On the way he sees Fortinbras's army marching to fight for a scrap of Poland and is ashamed of his own delay. Grief over her father's death drives Ophelia mad. Laertes returns from France demanding revenge, and Claudius turns his anger against Hamlet. News arrives that Hamlet is back in Denmark after his ship was attacked by pirates. Claudius and Laertes plan a fencing match in which Laertes will use a sharpened, poisoned blade, with a cup of poisoned wine as a back-up. Gertrude then reports that Ophelia has drowned.

Act 5. In the graveyard, Hamlet jokes with a gravedigger and holds the skull of Yorick, a jester he knew as a child. Ophelia's funeral arrives, and Hamlet and Laertes grapple in her grave. Hamlet tells Horatio that on the ship he found Claudius's letter and replaced it with one ordering the deaths of Rosencrantz and Guildenstern. He then accepts Laertes's challenge to the fencing match.

During the match, Gertrude drinks from the poisoned cup meant for Hamlet. Laertes wounds Hamlet with the poisoned blade; in a scuffle the swords are swapped and Hamlet wounds Laertes with it. Gertrude dies crying out that the drink is poisoned, and the dying Laertes confesses the plot and blames the king. Hamlet stabs Claudius with the poisoned sword and forces him to drink the rest of the wine. Laertes and Hamlet forgive each other, and Laertes dies. Hamlet stops Horatio from drinking the poison too, asks him to live and tell the true story, and gives his support to Fortinbras as the next king. Fortinbras arrives with ambassadors from England, who report that Rosencrantz and Guildenstern are dead, and he orders that Hamlet be carried off with military honours.

So the revenge is finally done, but it costs the lives of the whole royal family and of Polonius's family, and Denmark passes to a foreign prince whose father old King Hamlet had once defeated. Readers disagree about why Hamlet waits so long. One common reading is that he is a thinker who cannot turn thought into action. Another is that his caution is reasonable, since the Ghost could be lying. A third stresses his disgust with his mother's remarriage and with life itself. By Act 5 he talks of trusting providence and being ready for whatever comes, and many readers see the ending as Hamlet giving up control rather than finally seizing it. These readings are debated; Shakespeare left no comment on the play.

ul: Revenge and delay: Hamlet, Laertes and Fortinbras each have a father to avenge, and the play contrasts Hamlet's hesitation with the other two's readiness to act.
Appearance and reality: almost everyone hides something, from Claudius's crime and Hamlet's pretended madness to the spying of Polonius, Rosencrantz and Guildenstern.
Death and what follows it: the Ghost, the soliloquies and the graveyard scene keep returning to what death is and whether anything comes after it.
Corruption of the state: Claudius's secret murder is presented as a sickness spreading through Denmark, carried by repeated images of rot, disease and poison.
Madness: Hamlet's madness is at least partly an act, while Ophelia's is real, and the play leaves open how far Hamlet's is only performance.
Length: five acts; it is Shakespeare's longest play and runs about four hours uncut, so most stage and film versions trim it.
Text: three early versions survive (1603, 1604 and the 1623 First Folio); modern editions combine them.

Adaptations: well-known films include Laurence Olivier's (1948) and Kenneth Branagh's full-text version (1996); Tom Stoppard's play Rosencrantz and Guildenstern Are Dead retells it from the two courtiers' side.
Content: violent deaths, poisoning and a likely suicide (Ophelia), and speeches about suicide.

What teachers usually ask about: why Hamlet delays, whether his madness is real, the "To be, or not to be" soliloquy, how Hamlet treats Ophelia and Gertrude, and the role of the foils Laertes and Fortinbras.

check.q: Who does Hamlet kill by stabbing through a wall hanging in his mother's room?
check.why: He mistakes the hidden Polonius for Claudius.

check.q: How does Hamlet test whether the Ghost's story is true?
options: He questions Gertrude in front of the court
He has actors perform a play that copies the murder
He sends Horatio to search Claudius's rooms
check.why: Claudius's reaction to The Murder of Gonzago convinces Hamlet that he is guilty.

check.q: Who becomes ruler of Denmark at the end of the play?
check.why: The dying Hamlet gives his support to Fortinbras, the Prince of Norway, who arrives just after the deaths.

faq.a: According to the Ghost, Claudius poured poison into his ear while he slept in his orchard, then spread the story that a snake had bitten him. Claudius later admits the murder when he is alone trying to pray, confirming the Ghost's account.

Hamlet says in Act 1 that he will pretend to be mad, and he speaks sanely with Horatio throughout, so most readers see the madness as an act. Some argue that grief pushes him close to real breakdown at moments, such as his outburst at Ophelia's grave.

The play leaves it unclear. Gertrude describes her falling into a stream while gathering flowers and drowning without trying to save herself. The gravediggers and the priest suggest her death was suicide and that she is given a reduced funeral only because of her rank.
